title: The preview runner starts the product, captures it, and always stops the process
description:
SPIDR child 2 of task-f3edb8fb39ad42ce8980dae7d62b604c (architect-20a6d1eb, 2026-09-05). dependsOn child 1 task-40e52fa8a85a4921b97bee933b00403f for the refusal codes it raises.

WHAT THIS ROW OWNS: the daemon-side runner. Start the product's preview command in the project workspace, wait for its port, drive headless Chromium to the contract's journey entry URLs, capture one PNG per journey under `<project>/.moe-next/previews/<goalId>/<sha>/`, and write a `moe-preview-receipt/1` durable receipt. And - the part that actually matters - ALWAYS stop the child process. No UI in this row.

MEASURED AT HEAD df5bbfd5 (branch moe/work-2026-09-04) by architect-20a6d1eb:
- The gap is real: `grep -rn 'moe-preview-receipt' --include=*.ts apps/ packages/` = ZERO hits.
- REUSE, do not reinvent: `apps/daemon/src/orchestrator/verifier-process-runner.ts` (395 lines) already spawns a workspace command as a child process with timeouts and durable outcomes - read it before writing a second spawner. `apps/daemon/src/repository/landing-receipt-contracts.ts:20` defines `LANDING_RECEIPT_VERSION = "moe-landing-receipt/1"` and is the shape to mirror for `moe-preview-receipt/1`.
- `apps/daemon/src/orchestrator/node-verifier.ts` (230) and `node-lander.ts` (193) show how a runner's outcome becomes a durable receipt.

THE DEPENDENCY EDGE - owner decision 2026-09-05, and the first thing this row must do. `apps/daemon/package.json` has TWELVE workspace dependencies and ZERO devDependencies; Playwright is only a ROOT devDependency (`@playwright/test` 1.62.1, package.json:49) serving the e2e lane. The owner chose to make Playwright a real daemon dependency rather than degrade the capture. Global rail 7 therefore binds: the plan's FIRST step adds the dependency to apps/daemon/package.json, runs the workspace install so pnpm-lock.yaml carries the importer entry for @moe/daemon, and proves the edge with a compiled probe importing from the BARE specifier that typechecks exit 0 and is deleted in the same command. A root-barrel grep does NOT satisfy this. There is no escape hatch - this repo has no tsconfig "paths" and no project references, so a deep relative import fails TS6059. Declare BOTH apps/daemon/package.json and pnpm-lock.yaml as owned paths.

THE HARD PART IS THE PROCESS, NOT THE PICTURE. A preview that leaks a child process is worse than no preview: it holds the port, and the next preview fails to bind. The process must stop on APPROVE, on REJECT, on a 30-minute timeout, and on daemon shutdown, and the tests must assert the PID is actually gone rather than that a flag was set.
definitionOfDone: The runner resolves the preview command from the approved contract's deployment requirements, falling back to the workspace package.json `preview` -> `dev` -> `start` script in that order, and refuses PREVIEW_COMMAND_MISSING with its layer when none exists. A test asserts the fallback ORDER by giving a fixture workspace two of the three scripts and checking which ran - not merely that some command ran.

The port is taken from the contract when stated and otherwise detected from the child's stdout, with PREVIEW_START_TIMEOUT (code + layer asserted) when it never appears. Assert the timeout arm with a fixture product that starts and never listens, and use a short injected timeout so the arm does not actually wait 30 minutes.

A `moe-preview-receipt/1` durable receipt records {goalId, sha, url, pid, screenshots[], STARTED|REFUSED(code)} - mirroring the shape of `moe-landing-receipt/1` (repository/landing-receipt-contracts.ts:20). A test reads it back from the store and asserts every member, including that a REFUSED receipt carries its code and NO url.

SCREENSHOTS ARE REAL BYTES: against a fixture product (a tiny http server as the `preview` script) at least one PNG is written under `<project>/.moe-next/previews/<goalId>/<sha>/` and the test DECODES its bytes - asserting the PNG magic number and non-zero dimensions, never merely that a file exists at a path. Assert the receipt's screenshots[] entries point at the files actually written.

NO LEAKED PROCESS, asserted three ways by PID rather than by flag: the child is gone after APPROVE, after REJECT, and after a forced timeout. Use the same liveness check the J1 e2e uses for reaped pids. Add a fourth arm for daemon shutdown if the composition allows it; if it does not, say so explicitly in the completion record rather than silently covering three of four.
PREVIEW_GOAL_NOT_LANDED (code + layer) refuses a preview for a goal whose nodes are not all landed, asserted against a real store where one node is short - not a hand-built state.

The dependency edge is proven, not assumed: apps/daemon/package.json declares the browser dependency, pnpm-lock.yaml carries the importer entry for @moe/daemon, and a compiled probe importing the BARE specifier typechecks exit 0 (probe deleted in the same command). Quote all three (global rail 7).
Gates quoted with their `Test Files N passed` count lines: `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`, `pnpm typecheck`.
taskRails: NO UI. This row writes no control-room code. The Needs-you card, the status strip stage, the Runs receipt row and the Playwright journey are child 3's.

READ verifier-process-runner.ts BEFORE writing a spawner. If its timeout/kill/outcome machinery can be reused or extracted, do that and say so; a second independent process runner in the same daemon is how one of them comes to leak.
PROCESS CLEANUP IS THE SUBJECT, not a detail. Every exit path stops the child. Assert by PID liveness, never by an internal flag - a flag proves the code believed it killed something.
FEATURES ONLY (inherited): no security-boundary or policy work. The preview runs on the operator's machine and the workspace is trusted, per the documented v0.1 limitation.
Deployment to an environment is OUT of scope (the 'Containerized deployment' row owns it).

(c) COMPILED PROBE ON THE BARE SPECIFIER, deleted in the same command:

Same probe with the bogus bare specifier `playwright-does-not-exist-worker-8c5af680` -> EXIT 1 with `src/preview/edge-probe-negative.ts(1,26): error TS2307: Cannot find module ... or its corresponding type declarations.` So the leg really resolves bare specifiers; the green above is not vacuous. Chromium is on the host: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\ms-playwright` holds `chromium-1234`, `chromium_headless_shell-1234`, `ffmpeg-1011`, `winldd-1007`. Step 6's capture will not need a download.

THE INSTALL NEARLY TOOK THE FLEET DOWN — recorded because the next agent to touch a manifest here will hit it. `pnpm install` (filtered AND unfiltered) failed with `ERR_PNPM_ABORTED_REMOVE_MODULES_DIR_NO_TTY`. I did NOT set `confirmModulesPurge=false`: reading pnpm.mjs:156868, `removeContentsOfDir2` skips dot-entries EXCEPT any dir equal to `virtualStoreDir`, so a root purge rimrafs `node_modules/.pnpm` — the whole 385-package virtual store — which would break every live seat's gate. Instrumenting an out-of-tree COPY of pnpm.mjs (it throws before deleting, so the diagnostic run is safe) named the real cause: `ERR_PNPM_UNEXPECTED_STORE`. `.modules.yaml` records `storeDir = C:\Users\Yaron\AppData\Local\pnpm\store\v11` but `pnpm store path` now resolves `D:\.pnpm-store\v11`, and `checkCompatibility` then pushes all 20 importers INCLUDING the root onto `importersToPurge`. FIX, no purge, 3.8s: `pnpm install --prefer-offline --store-dir "C:\Users\Yaron\AppData\Local\pnpm\store\v11"` -> `resolved 385, reused 323, downloaded 2, added 0, done`, EXIT 0.

SECOND TRAP, disclosed because it is a fleet hazard: `node_modules/.pnpm-workspace-state-v1.json` carries `lastValidatedTimestamp`, and a manifest newer than it makes `runDepsStatusCheck` auto-run `pnpm install` before ANY `pnpm --filter <pkg> <script>`. While that install was failing, EVERY seat's gate failed with a `runDepsStatusCheck` stack trace and zero tsc output. I proved the window is closed: `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon exec node -e "console.log('FILTER_OK')"` prints FILTER_OK. Both hazards written to Serena as `gotcha-pnpm-install-here-needs-an-explicit-store-dir`.

Peer dirt noted, untouched: 47 foreign dirty paths including `?? apps/daemon/src/repository/deployment/` and `.vite`/`.vite-temp` caches under `apps/daemon/node_modules`. Not reverted, not stashed, not staged.

implementationPlan.description: READ THE EXISTING RUNNER BEFORE WRITING ONE (task rail 2). `apps/daemon/src/orchestrator/verifier-process-runner.ts` (395 lines) already spawns a workspace command with everything this row needs: injectable `spawn`, `timeoutMs`, `killGraceMs` and `killProcessGroup` (options at :49-55), a `killStragglersBestEffort` that SIGKILLs the process GROUP via `killProcessGroup(-child.pid, "SIGKILL")` (:187-189), and timer cleanup on every exit path (:110-114). In a step note, state explicitly whether the preview reuses it, extracts a shared core from it, or must spawn separately — and if separately, say exactly which behaviour differs (a long-lived server that must OUTLIVE the call, versus a test command that runs to completion, is the likely answer). A second independent process runner in the same daemon is how one of them comes to leak, so this decision is recorded rather than made silently.
implementationPlan.note:
READ-ONLY STEP. Decision: SPAWN SEPARATELY, reuse the two seams that matter. No production file changed.

THE DECISION, and the exact behaviour that differs. `createVerifierProcessRunner`'s public surface is `VerifierProcessRunner = (brief: NodeMission) => Promise<VerifierRunCapture>` (process-runner-lifecycle.ts:29-33). That promise resolves ONLY from `finish()`, and every path into `finish()` runs off `child.on("close")`, `child.on("exit")` + `drainGraceMs`, or a termination (verifier-process-runner.ts:202-217). It is structurally "run to completion and hand back the capture". A preview server never completes: `await runner(brief)` on `npm run preview` would sit until `timeoutMs` and then report the run as a TIMEOUT kill. So the preview cannot call `run()` — not a style preference, a lifecycle mismatch. The preview needs a handle that RETURNS while the child is still listening, is driven by the browser, and is stopped later by an operator decision that may arrive minutes afterwards.

WHY NOT EXTRACT THE KILL CORE. Tempting — `killTree` is exactly the containment I need — but it is not separable as it stands: it closes over `child`, `childExited`, `treeKillConfirmed`, `killHelper`, `settled`, and calls `failContainment`/`maybeFinishTermination`, which in turn set `closed` on the whole runner and push onto `containmentFailures` for `close()` to throw as an AggregateError. Lifting it means restructuring a 395-line file that (a) this row does not own, (b) three other rows are editing in this shared checkout right now, and (c) is covered by its own suite whose containment arms drive those exact internals. Trading a clean extraction for a chance of reddening a foreign suite mid-flight is the wrong trade. Recorded here rather than decided silently, per task rail 2.

WHAT I DO REUSE, so this is not a second runner pretending to be new:
- `probeProcessAlive(pid, kill)` from `orchestrator/process-runner-lifecycle.ts:47` — the daemon's existing liveness seam, ESRCH=dead / EPERM=ALIVE / anything else rethrown. I write no second probe. This is also what the tests assert through (see below).
- The kill STRATEGY is copied deliberately and cited: win32 gets `taskkill.exe /pid <n> /T /F` resolved through SYSTEMROOT (verifier-process-runner.ts:255-262) because a detached child's descendants survive a bare `child.kill()`; POSIX gets `killProcessGroup(-child.pid, "SIGKILL")` against the GROUP (:298), with ESRCH treated as containment REACHED, not failed (:302-306). `detached: platform !== "win32"` (:153) is what makes the negative pid address a group at all.
- Injectable `spawn`, `timeoutMs`, `killGraceMs`, `killProcessGroup`, `platform` — same option names as `VerifierProcessRunnerOptions:39-55`, so the two runners read alike.
- Receipt shape and discipline from `repository/landing-receipt-contracts.ts` + `repository/landing-ledger.ts`: exact-key decoder, `hash([VERSION, "receipt-id", ...])` deterministic id (:127-131), write through `store.commitExpectedVersionDecision` under a reserved principal on a SIDE aggregate, and a read-back that re-validates the bytes AND that the decision's `targetAggregateId` matches (landing-ledger.ts:75-88). Replay-safety comes free from the same idempotence: `recordLandingReceipt` returns `replayed:true` on a second call with the same id (:179-180).

PLAN/REALITY CONFLICT FOUND, resolved without narrowing the DoD. Step 7 says to use `pidReaped` from `tests/e2e/foundation/orphan-reap.ts`. apps/daemon CANNOT import it: `apps/daemon/tsconfig.json` sets `"rootDir": "src"` and `"include": ["src/**/*.ts"]`, so a `tests/e2e/**` import is TS6059, the same wall global rail 7 names. I keep the SEMANTICS, which is what the clause is protecting: `orphan-reap.ts:1-17` documents that `taskkill /T /F` returns when the kill is REQUESTED, not when the OS has reaped, and that a killed pid stays visible for 68-100ms (8/8 samples) and longer under load — so sampling liveness immediately after a kill grades the sampling instant, not the containment claim. My arms therefore poll to a budget exactly like `pidReaped` (200 polls x 50ms, answer false rather than throw) but call `probeProcessAlive` from the PRODUCTION module instead of `pidIsAlive` from the e2e harness. Net effect: same anti-flake property, one fewer liveness probe in the repo, and the test asserts through a production surface rather than a helper I wrote.

SEAMS MEASURED FOR THE LATER STEPS, so no step re-derives them:
- Store fixtures: `openStore`, `closeStores`, `hex64`, `PROJECT_ID` from `review/review-test-fixtures.js` (landing-ledger.test.ts:3); real-world driver `openStore`, `driveThrough`, `GOAL_ID`, `PROJECT_ID` from `bootstrap/bootstrap-test-fixtures.js` and `seedReviewAcceptance`/`seedLandingReceipt` from `goals/goal-closure-test-fixtures.js` (goal-landing-facts.test.ts:14-18). The seed world's activated graph names `node-a`.
- PREVIEW_GOAL_NOT_LANDED needs ALL nodes landed; `goalHasLandedCommit` (goal-landing-facts.ts:112) answers ANY, and

implementationPlan.description: THE RECEIPT CONTRACT, in a new apps/daemon/src/preview/preview-receipt-contracts.ts, mirroring apps/daemon/src/repository/landing-receipt-contracts.ts. Export `PREVIEW_RECEIPT_VERSION = "moe-preview-receipt/1"`, its internal command kind, and a deterministic receipt-id function of (projectId, goalId, sha) — the landing receipt derives its id from the verifier receipt precisely so "a wrapper restart lands nothing twice" (node-lander.ts:25-26), and the preview needs the same property. Carry the landing contract's discipline verbatim in the type: a preview that did not start is recorded as a REFUSED receipt WITH ITS CODE, never as an absent receipt — "an absent landing is not a false one" (landing-receipt-contracts.ts header). Members: goalId, sha, url, pid, screenshots[], and STARTED | REFUSED(code). Ship the `.js` bridge (`export * from "./preview-receipt-contracts.ts";`) or the daemon dies at boot with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND.
implementationPlan.note:
THE RECEIPT CONTRACT, plus the ledger that makes it durable. Both under the per-file cap: preview-receipt-contracts.ts = 207 lines, preview-ledger.ts = 154.

WHY TWO FILES, not one. `landing-receipt-contracts.ts` (236) and `landing-ledger.ts` are two files for the same reason: the CONTRACT reads nothing and writes nothing (pure shapes + decoder + id), while the LEDGER holds the store. Folding them would put a `@moe/store` import in the vocabulary and take the pair past 350 lines. Same split, same names.

WHAT preview-receipt-contracts.ts EXPORTS:
- `PREVIEW_RECEIPT_VERSION = "moe-preview-receipt/1"`, `PREVIEW_RECEIPT_COMMAND_KIND = "internal.preview.run_receipt"` (an `internal.*` kind, never dispatched from the wire — same discipline as `LANDING_RECEIPT_COMMAND_KIND`), `PREVIEW_RUNNER_PRINCIPAL_ID = "daemon:preview-runner"`.
- `previewReceiptId(projectId, goalId, sha)` — `sha256(JSON.stringify([VERSION, "receipt-id", projectId, goalId, sha]))`, the same construction as `landingReceiptId` (landing-receipt-contracts.ts:127-131). The step asked for the restart-idempotence property the landing id exists for; the preview needs it for a SHARPER reason than "lands nothing twice", and I wrote that reason into the header: the run behind this receipt spawns a server that BINDS A PORT, so a second id would start a second server that fails to bind against the first.
- `previewAggregateId(goalId) = "preview:<goalId>"` — beside the goal, never on it, mirroring `landingAggregateId`. Starting a preview must not move a version the planner or reviewer is reading against.
- `previewCaptureDirectory(goalId, sha) = ".moe-next/previews/<goalId>/<sha>"` — one statement of the path, so step 6's writer and this decoder cannot disagree about where captures live.
- `PreviewReceiptV1` with exactly the members the DoD names: goalId, sha, url, pid, screenshots[], outcome STARTED | REFUSED, plus code/projectId/receiptId/decidedAt/version.
- `decodePreviewReceiptBytes` (exact-key, prototype-null objects only) and `previewReceiptLayer`.

THE REFUSAL DISCIPLINE IS STRUCTURAL, which is the part worth reviewing. DoD 3 requires a REFUSED receipt to carry its code and NO url. I did not write that as two one-way guards — I wrote it as three EQUIVALENCES the decoder refuses on:
  started !== (url !== null) || started !== (pid !== null) || started === (code !== null)
So neither shape can be half-built in either direction: a STARTED receipt missing its url refuses just as loudly as a REFUSED one that still advertises one. A fourth guard refuses a REFUSED receipt that carries screenshots — pictures of a product that never started. The url is what an operator CLICKS; a refusal that still offered one would send them to a port nothing is listening on.

THE LAYER IS DERIVED, NEVER STORED. `previewReceiptLayer` re-reads `PREVIEW_CODE_LAYERS` from task-40e52fa8's vocabulary rather than persisting a layer alongside the code, and the decoder refuses any `code` not `in PREVIEW_CODE_LAYERS`. So there is exactly ONE statement of which layer answers which code in the whole preview path, and a receipt cannot contradict the vocabulary. This is the same reason `previewRefusal(code)` takes no layer argument (preview-contracts.ts:142).

PATH CONTAINMENT IS CHECKED ON THE READ, not only the write. `parseScreenshots` refuses any entry whose path does not start with `<captureDirectory>/`, or contains `..` or a backslash, or repeats a path already seen. Checking it in the DECODER means a receipt cannot advertise another run's pictures even if a future writer got it wrong — containment survives the module that produced it. Step 6 adds the writer-side check.

preview-ledger.ts mirrors `landing-ledger.ts` move for move: `ownDecision` re-checks the decision's key against the record (principal, kind, commandId, projectId, EFFECTS_COMMITTED) rather than trusting the lookup (landing-ledger.ts:57-73); `readPreviewReceipt` additionally requires `decision.targetAggregateId === previewAggregateId(receipt.goalId)`; `recordPreviewReceipt` validates the bytes through the decoder BEFORE committing them (so a record the decoder would refuse never reaches the store and cannot poison the read-back forever), commits through `store.commitExpectedVersionDecision`, and then READS THE RECEIPT BACK, returning the persisted bytes rather than the intended object. Replay returns `{ok:true, replayed:true}` with the FIRST receipt.

TWO API CORRECTIONS caught by the typecheck rather than by assumption: the store field is `decision.resultBytes`, not `committedResultBytes` (that is the WRITE-side input name on `commitExpectedVersionDecision`; `EffectsCommittedDecision` exposes `resultBytes` — store-contracts.ts:121-134), and `CommandDecisionRecord` needed a type import. Both fixed.

BRIDGES SHIPPED: `preview-receipt-contracts.js` and `preview-ledger.js`, each `export * from "./<name>.ts";` matching the existing `preview-contracts.js` byte pattern. Without them the daemon dies at boot with ERR_MODULE_N

implementationPlan.description: COMMAND RESOLUTION AND PORT DETECTION, in a new apps/daemon/src/preview/preview-runner.ts. Resolve the preview command from the approved contract's deployment requirements, falling back to the workspace package.json scripts `preview` -> `dev` -> `start` IN THAT ORDER, refusing PREVIEW_COMMAND_MISSING (code + layer from task-40e52fa8's contract module) when none exists. Take the port from the contract when stated, otherwise detect it from the child's stdout, refusing PREVIEW_START_TIMEOUT when it never appears. Refuse PREVIEW_GOAL_NOT_LANDED when the goal's nodes are not all landed. Keep the timeout INJECTABLE with a 30-minute production default, exactly as verifier-process-runner does — a test that actually waits 30 minutes will be deleted by whoever inherits it.
implementationPlan.note:
COMMAND RESOLUTION, PORT DETECTION, THE LANDED GATE, AND THE PROCESS. Four production modules, every one under the cap: preview-command-resolution 170, preview-goal-landing 87, preview-process 252, preview-runner 180. One file would have been ~690 lines, so the split is the per-file cap, not preference; each is one responsibility with its own header.

THE FALLBACK ORDER, and why it is not cosmetic. `PREVIEW_SCRIPT_ORDER = ["preview","dev","start"]` is a single frozen constant, and `resolvePreviewCommand` walks it. The header records WHY the order matters, so a future reader does not "simplify" it: all three usually exist in a real product and they mean different things — `preview` serves a BUILT artifact, `dev` serves a hot-reloading one, `start` may serve production and may block on configuration the operator lacks. Picking the wrong one shows the operator a picture of something other than what was built. A script present but EMPTY (`"dev": ""`) is treated as ABSENT: spawning an empty command line would surface as a start timeout twenty-nine minutes later instead of a refusal now.

MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED — the contract carries no preview fields. `ProductContractV2Requirement` is `{statement, dependsOnRequirementIds, priority, requirementId, supersedesRequirementId}` (product-contract-v2-contract.ts:95-100) and `ProductContractV2Journey` is `{statement, criterionIds, journeyId, userJobId}` (:89-93). There is NO command field, NO port field and NO url field anywhere in the revision. So "resolve from the contract's deployment requirements" can only mean reading the free-prose `statement`, and I made that an explicit, narrow, documented DIRECTIVE rather than a guess: `preview command: <cmd>`, `preview port: <n>` in a deployment statement, `preview path: /checkout` in a JOURNEY statement (default "/"). Deliberately narrow, and the header says why: guessing a command out of English would let "must not be previewed with the dev server" start the dev server, so an unrecognised statement contributes NOTHING. Contract beats scripts because the approved contract is the product's own statement of how it is served; the script scan is only what happens when it does not say.

PORT DETECTION IS ANCHORED ON AN ORIGIN, NOT ON A NUMBER. `detectPreviewPort` matches `https?://(localhost|127.0.0.1|[::1]|0.0.0.0):<port>` — the shape Vite, Next, Astro and http-server all print. A bare-number scan would read "compiled 42 modules in 1200ms" as port 42 and drive the browser at whatever else is listening there. `0.0.0.0` is normalised to `127.0.0.1` because it is a BIND address, never a connect address, and navigating to it fails on Windows.

ANSWERABLE, NOT MERELY SPAWNED — a design change I made against the plan's literal wording, disclosed here. The plan reads "port from the contract when stated, otherwise detected from stdout, with PREVIEW_START_TIMEOUT when it never appears". Implemented literally, a STATED port would return the instant the child had a pid, so the timeout arm could never fire on that branch and a contract-stated port would hand the browser an origin nothing was listening on. Both branches therefore end at the same loopback TCP probe (`portAccepts`), so a product that starts and never listens reaches PREVIEW_START_TIMEOUT whether its port was stated or detected. Strictly stronger than the clause; nothing in the DoD is narrowed.

THE LANDED GATE IS ALL-NODES, AND IT IS NOT `goalHasLandedCommit`. That function answers "at least ONE node landed" (goal-landing-facts.ts:112) — right for offering a PUBLISH, wrong for a preview, where a goal one node short shows a product missing exactly that node's work. Its `nodeOwners`/`landedGoals` walk is module-private, so rather than widen a foreign file's exports mid-flight in a shared checkout, `readGoalLandingStatus` reads the SAME TWO PUBLIC SEAMS it reads: `activeCompiledGraphs(store, projectId, LANDABLE_LIFECYCLES, ledger)` (compiled-node-source.ts:89) and `readReviewLedgers`. Same sources, ALL instead of ANY. It returns `{allLanded, missing[], nodes[]}` so a refusal can say WHICH node is short. Drive headless Chromium to the contract's journey entry URLs and write one PNG per journey under `<project>/.moe-next/previews/<goalId>/<sha>/`. THE TEST DECODES THE BYTES: assert the PNG magic number (89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A) and non-zero dimensions — never merely that a file exists at a path, which passes on a zero-byte file the browser failed to write. Assert the receipt's screenshots[] entries name exactly the files actually written, so a receipt cannot advertise a capture that is not on disk. Confirm the paths stay inside the goal's own directory: the capture writes only under `<project>/.moe-next/previews/<goalId>/<sha>/`, and a goalId or sha that would escape that prefix is refused rather than joined.
implementationPlan.note:
REAL BYTES FROM A REAL CHROMIUM. `npx vitest run --root . --config package.json src/preview/` -> `Test Files 5 passed (5)` / `Tests 69 passed (69)`, 38.29s.

THE ARMS DECODE, THEY DO NOT STAT. `decodePng` reads the 8-byte signature AND pulls the width from bytes 16-19 and the height from 20-23 of the IHDR chunk, both big-endian — so "non-zero dimensions" is a claim about the IMAGE, not about the file's length. Five capture arms plus one end-to-end runner arm.

THE CONTROL THAT MAKES THE OTHERS MEAN SOMETHING: "proves the decode arm is not vacuous: a zero-byte file fails the same assertion" writes `Buffer.alloc(0)` to a .png, asserts `existsSync(path) === true`, then asserts `decodePng` THROWS on it. That is the step-8 drill's outcome already pinned as a permanent committed arm rather than a transcript: the zero-byte file a failed capture leaves behind passes a file-exists check and fails this one, in the same test file, forever.

CAPTURE ARMS: (1) one journey -> a PNG whose magic matches `PNG_MAGIC` byte for byte, width>0, height>0, byteLength>1000 (a 1280x720 viewport shot; a truncated write cannot reach that). (2) two journeys -> exactly `<prefix>journey-home.png` and `<prefix>journey-checkout.png` where prefix is `previewCaptureDirectory(...)`, EVERY entry re-decoded, plus `expect(first).not.toBe(second)` on the base64 — the fixture serves the path in the document, so identical bytes would mean the second navigation never happened and both shots are of the same page. (3) containment. (4) an unreachable origin returns an EMPTY roster and writes no file — the receipt can never advertise a capture that is not on disk.

CONTAINMENT IS TWO CHECKS AT TWO LAYERS, and both REFUSE rather than sanitise. The runner refuses an escaping goalId or sha before any join (`containedSegment`); the capture refuses an escaping journeyRef (`containedRef`). A skipped ref is absent from the returned roster, so it cannot be advertised. Arm 3 feeds `../../escaped`, `sub/dir` and `journey-ok` and asserts the roster is exactly `["journey-ok"]` AND that no `escaped.png` exists in the workspace or its PARENT. Sanitising instead of refusing is how a capture ends up somewhere nobody looks for it.

A CORRUPTION I INTRODUCED AND CAUGHT — worth recording because it was invisible to the tests. Writing these guards through a bash heredoc put RAW control bytes into two production files: `preview-runner.ts` ended up with a literal NUL inside `!value.includes("\0")` where I had written `" "`, and a retry mangled `preview-capture.ts` into `/[\s\x00-\x1f]/u` with raw 0x00 and 0x1f BYTES in the source. `grep` reported "Binary file matches", which is how I noticed. Both files now measure `NUL bytes: 0, control bytes: 0`. Crucially THE TESTS WERE GREEN THROUGHOUT: the existing arms feed `../escape`, `a/b`, `a\b`, `..` and none exercised the whitespace branch, so a guard that had silently become "reject NUL" instead of "reject space" passed. Fixed properly with a named, commented `UNSAFE_SEGMENT = /[�-\s/\\<>:"|?*]/u` in both files — escape sequences, not raw bytes — now covering control chars, whitespace, both separators and the Windows-reserved set (which would otherwise make a write fail on one platform and succeed on another). LESSON: never author source containing escape sequences through a bash heredoc; use the Write/Edit tools or a file-based script.

THE SHIPPED COMPOSITION IS THE REAL ONE. `PreviewRunnerConfig.capture` is now OPTIONAL and defaults to `capturePreviewJourneys`, so `runPreview` launches Chromium in production. The new end-to-end arm passes `capture: undefined` explicitly to take that default: it lands `node-a`, starts the real fixture server, drives the real browser at two contract-stated journeys, then READS THE RECEIPT BACK FROM THE STORE (not from the return value) and asserts outcome STARTED, code null, url === the handle's origin, pid === the handle's pid, goalId, sha, and `screenshots[]` exactly `[<prefix>journey-home.png, <prefix>journey-checkout.png]` — then opens each advertised file and decodes its PNG header and dimensions. That closes DoD 4's "assert the receipt's screenshots[] entries point at the files actually written": the roster and the bytes are checked against each other, so neither can lie alone. Without the default the port's only implementation would have lived in a test, making every runner arm a test of the test.

And the browser close sits in a `finally` that runs on the throwing path — a leaked Chromium is a leaked process, which is this row's whole subject; page and context closes are `.catch(() => undefined)` so a close failure cannot mask the capture's own outcome.

implementationPlan.description: NO LEAKED PROCESS — the subject of this row (task rail 3), asserted by PID and never by a flag. A flag proves the code BELIEVED it killed something. Arms: the child is gone after APPROVE, after REJECT, and after a forced timeout. Use the same liveness check the J1 e2e uses for reaped pids (tests/e2e/foundation has a `pidReaped` helper — reuse it rather than inventing a second liveness probe). On Windows a detached child's descendants survive a bare `child.kill()`, which is why verifier-process-runner signals the process GROUP; assert the SERVER's port is free after the kill, not only that the direct pid is gone, because a surviving grandchild holding the port is exactly the failure that makes the next preview unable to bind. FOURTH ARM — daemon shutdown: add it if the composition allows a shutdown hook; if it does not, say so EXPLICITLY in the completion record rather than silently shipping three of four (the parent's roll-up step 2 checks for this admission).
implementationPlan.note:
FOUR ARMS, ALL FOUR PRESENT — and the port assertion CAUGHT A REAL LEAK. `src/preview/` -> `Test Files 6 passed (6)` / `Tests 75 passed (75)`, 32.83s.

THE BUG THE PLAN PREDICTED, found and fixed. On the first run FOUR of six arms failed, every one on `awaitPortFree === false`: the pid was gone and THE PORT WAS STILL BOUND. Cause, in my own step-4 code: `killTree` spawned `taskkill /pid <n> /T /F`, `unref`'d it, and IMMEDIATELY called `child.kill("SIGKILL")` without waiting. `shell: true` makes the direct child `cmd.exe` and the server its GRANDCHILD, so killing the shell first orphaned node before taskkill had walked the tree. Every pid assertion passed — cmd.exe really was gone — while the next preview would have been unable to bind. THAT IS EXACTLY THE FAILURE THE PLAN'S RISK NOTE NAMED, and only the port check saw it. Fix: `killTree` is now async and AWAITS taskkill's `close` (`awaitTreeKill`), treating exit 0 or 128 as the tree gone (128 is "no running instance" — already dead is the outcome the call exists to reach) and falling back to the direct kill only when the walk could not run or timed out. `stop()` awaits it. If I had asserted only by pid, as a weaker plan would have, this row would have shipped the leak.

ARM 1 — APPROVE. ARM 2 — REJECT. Both drive a real server through `supervisor.decide(receiptId, ...)`, then assert the pid is gone AND the port is free AND the roster is empty. Arm 2 exists on its own because a runner that cleaned up only on the happy path would leak on every REJECTED preview — the common case.

ARM 3 — FORCED TIMEOUT. The refusal path is the likeliest to leak because nothing downstream holds a handle to stop, so `startPreviewProcess` is driven directly with a wrapped REAL spawn that records the pid (the child genuinely starts; "it is gone" is a claim about a process that really existed). `SILENT_SERVER` starts and never listens; `startTimeoutMs: 1_200`; the arm asserts code PREVIEW_START_TIMEOUT and then that the pid left the table.

ARM 4 — DAEMON SHUTDOWN IS PRESENT, not admitted-absent. The plan allowed reporting that the composition does not permit it; I made the composition permit it instead, which is the better answer. `createPreviewSupervisor` (preview-supervisor.ts, 118 lines) owns the live roster, so the daemon has exactly ONE thing to close. `close()` sweeps every live preview and refuses to start more. The arm holds TWO previews open at once and asserts both pids gone and both ports free, so it proves a SWEEP rather than one lucky stop. A fifth arm covers the race a roster-based sweep would otherwise miss: a `start()` that lands AFTER `close()` has already swept would join a roster nobody will sweep again, so it stops itself instead — asserted by pid and port.

ASSERTED BY PID, NEVER BY A FLAG. `alive()` calls `probeProcessAlive` from `orchestrator/process-runner-lifecycle.ts:47` — PRODUCTION code I did not write — and every arm polls to a budget rather than sampling once, because `taskkill /T /F` returns when the kill is REQUESTED, not when the OS has reaped (orphan-reap.ts:1-17 measures 68-100ms idle and longer under load); sampling immediately grades the sampling instant, not the containment claim. `startLive` asserts the PRECONDITIONS first — `alive(pid) === true` and `portAccepts(port) === true` — so no arm can pass by never having started anything.

THE PLAN'S `pidReaped` CLAUSE, and why the import is impossible. Step 7 says to reuse `tests/e2e/foundation/orphan-reap.ts`. It cannot be imported: `apps/daemon/tsconfig.json` sets `"rootDir": "src"` and `"include": ["src/**/*.ts"]`, so a `tests/e2e/**` import is TS6059 — the same wall global rail 7 documents, with no `paths` and no project references to route around it. I kept the SEMANTICS exactly (200 polls x 50ms, answers false rather than throwing so the caller names the surviving pid) in `awaitPidGone`, over the PRODUCTION probe rather than the e2e harness's `pidIsAlive`. Net: same anti-flake property, one fewer liveness probe in the repo, and the assertion runs through a production surface instead of a helper I wrote. The reasoning is in the test file's header so a reader does not think the clause was skipped.

SUPERVISOR DESIGN NOTES. Four ways a preview ends and all four run the same `stopPreview`: APPROVE, REJECT, a start that never became answerable (already stopped inside `startPreviewProcess`), and shutdown. `forget()` removes an entry from the roster BEFORE stopping it, so a decision and a shutdown racing the same preview stop it once between them rather than both waiting; `stop()` is memoised per handle, so a double call is free. APPROVE and REJECT are the SAME instruction to the process — what differs is what the graph is told afterwards, which is child 3's, not this row's. `close()` does not throw on a straggler: its caller is the daemon on its way down, and making shutdown throw would take the daemon down harder without killing anything extra — an escaped process is caught by the pid assertions

TWO REAL DEFECTS FOUND IN MY OWN CODE BY THE ADVERSARIAL PASS, both fixed with arms:

Two concurrent `supervisor.start` calls for the same revision both passed the landed gate and both spawned a server; the second could not bind the port the first took and refused PREVIEW_START_TIMEOUT — a preview that failed for no reason an operator could act on. The receipt's idempotence does NOT prevent this: it dedupes the RECORD, by which time two processes are running. THE PORT ASSERTION CAUGHT A REAL LEAK. My first killTree spawned `taskkill /T /F` and immediately SIGKILLed the shell without waiting. `shell: true` makes the direct child cmd.exe and the server its GRANDCHILD, so the shell died first and orphaned node: every PID assertion passed while the port stayed BOUND. Fixed by awaiting taskkill's exit (0 or 128) before any fallback kill. Asserting only by pid would have shipped it.

The plan permitted admitting the 4th was unreachable; instead I made the composition allow it (createPreviewSupervisor owns the live roster, close() sweeps it, arm holds two previews open).
